nameStory: The autumn crocus earned its quirky nickname "naked ladies" (or "naked boys") because of its unusual habit of blooming stark naked - the flowers push up through the soil in fall with absolutely no leaves in sight! The leaves don't appear until the following spring, making these purple blooms look like they forgot to get dressed before coming to the garden party.
description: Autumn crocus is a small bulbous plant that puts on a backwards show compared to most flowers. In fall, delicate purple or pink crocus-like flowers emerge directly from bare ground on short stems, typically reaching 4-6 inches tall. The strap-shaped leaves don't appear until spring, growing much taller than the flowers before dying back in summer. Despite its name and appearance, it's not a true crocus at all, but belongs to an entirely different plant family.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Six purple to pink petals form a goblet shape, emerging directly from soil in fall with no visible leaves - the flowers feel delicate and papery to the touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Broad, strap-like green leaves appear only in spring, growing 8-12 inches tall before dying back completely by summer - they feel thick and somewhat rubbery

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Flowers pop up individually or in small clusters directly from underground bulbs with no visible stem or foliage during bloom time

idTips.label: Timing
idTips.description: Blooms exclusively in fall (September-October) when most other flowers are finished, making the leafless purple blooms unmistakable

habitat: Found in cultivated gardens, naturalized lawns, and occasionally escaped to meadows and grassy areas throughout New England. Prefers well-drained soil and partial to full sun. Most commonly encountered as a garden ornamental that has spread beyond its original planting site.

seasonality.spring: Only the leaves are visible - broad, strap-shaped green foliage emerges and grows quite tall, with no flowers present.
seasonality.summer: Completely dormant with no visible parts above ground - both leaves and flowers are absent during the hot months.
seasonality.fall: The magic happens - purple crocus-like flowers emerge from bare soil with no leaves, blooming September through October.
seasonality.winter: Dormant underground with no visible growth, though bulbs may be preparing for spring leaf emergence.

funFact: This plant is a master of botanical time travel - it blooms with energy stored from leaves that grew six months earlier, then produces next year's food with leaves that won't appear until six months later!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with true fall-blooming crocuses, but autumn crocus flowers are larger and have six stamens instead of three. Memory trick: "Six stamens signals fake saffron" - true crocuses (which can produce saffron) have only three stamens.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "meadow saffron," this plant is NOT the source of real saffron spice and is actually quite toxic if eaten. The name confusion has led to accidental poisonings. Real saffron comes from a true crocus species, Crocus sativus.
compareHints: Autumn crocus is the only member of its genus commonly found in New England gardens. It differs from related plants in the bellwort family by its fall blooming time and crocus-like flowers - most other family members bloom in spring and have very different flower shapes. The naked autumn flowering habit is virtually unique among New England bulbs.
